evidence: src/infrastructure/http/createHttpApp.ts: createHttpApp builds OrderController and CatalogueController from HttpAppDependencies and passes them to createRouter along with requireStaff(deps.staffApiKey)

src/infrastructure/http/routes.ts: createRouter(controllers: Controllers, staffOnly: RequestHandler) only maps paths to controller handlers such as orders.place, orders.changeStatus('pack') and catalogue.listStockLevels
src/infrastructure/http/routes.ts: the staff guard is injected as the staffOnly parameter rather than implemented here; it is attached per route under /staff
src/infrastructure/http/routes.ts: /orders/:id/cancel and /staff/orders/:id/cancel both call orders.changeStatus('cancel'), so the cancel behaviour lives in one place
src/infrastructure/http/createHttpApp.ts: the /health check is an app-level endpoint with no controller, kept next to the other app-wide middleware
parsedVerdict.reasoning: The two files serve one concern: building the Express HTTP layer. createHttpApp.ts sets up the app (body parser, health check, not-found and error handlers) and builds the controllers from the use cases. routes.ts maps paths to controller handlers. Both files go through the Controllers interface and the injected staffOnly guard, and neither bypasses the controllers to call use cases or domain logic directly. The staff check is implemented once (requireStaff) and passed in as a parameter. routes.ts attaches it to each /staff route individually rather than mounting a /staff sub-router, which is a small style point, not a rule defined twice. Both cancel routes call the same orders.changeStatus('cancel') handler, so no business rule is repeated. /health lives in createHttpApp.ts because it is an app-level check with no controller behind it, which is a reasonable placement and not a split concern.
